nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Jewfish
Scientific Name: Epinephelus itajara

Other Common Names:  Spotted jewfish, giant seabass, guasa, mero

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Serranidae

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Lichenstein).
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)
	Revision date should be checked

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Food fish throughout its range and sold as grouper in limited commercial fishery (2401).  Fishery managers of Florida territorial and U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone waters have recognized the jewfish's susceptibility to overfishing and have recently banned (1990) all harvest of jewfish from waters under their jurisdictions (2402).
Recreational:  Historically easily captured by anglers and SCUBA divers, but now banned (1990) from sport fishery in Florida waters (2401; 2402).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Introduction:  Jewfish are one of the largest teleostean top predators within the Indian River Lagoon and adjacent waters, commonly encountered in ocean inlets, mangrove forests, seagrass meadows and nearshore ocean reefs (848, 993).  Juveniles occur around structures within the lagoon, such as seagrass, mangrove prop roots and rock ledges (2365).  Adults prefer structures associated with deeper water (generally over 3 m depths, but less than 55 m) both within the lagoon and adjacent continental shelf (2401).  Due to its size and broad diet of crustaceans and fishes (2389; 2361; 2401) jewfish may influence mortality rates in certain crustacean and fish populations where it is common as an apical predator.
Indicator:  None known.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Commonly encountered on reef formations from eastern Florida, Gulf of Mexico to southeastern Brazil and in the eastern Pacific from Costa Rica to Peru (2401).  Extralimital occurrence to Virginia (2406).
Within Study Area:  Occurs in Indian River Lagoon seagrass and mangrove estuarine habitats, particularly as a juvenile (848, 993), primarily south of 28 00'N.  Adults are found in deeper basins within the Indian River Lagoon typically near ocean inlets and on nearshore ocean reefs at depths less than 55 m (848; Gilmore, 1972-84 unpubl. field notes Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution).
Life Mode:  A very large solitary residential neritic and estuarine ambush predator (size to 317 kg and over 1.8 m SL: Smith 1971).  Forms predictable aggregations during spawning around reef structure on the continental shelf (2403; 2401).  Highly vulnerable to fishery pressure due to slow growth, longevity, and presumed low natural mortality as populations of cohorts reach maximum biomass at relatively old ages (2402).
Mobility and Migration: Adults make limited migrations to spawning sites and are otherwise relatively sedentary with single individuals having been observed at specific reef formations over multiple annual cycles (2410; 2403; 2401; 2402).  Juveniles move from coastal and estuarine nursery grounds to deeper estuarine or continental shelf reefs upon maturation (2402).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Epinephelus itajara associates with objects rising above the ocean or estuarine bottom as newly settled post larvae or juveniles.  These objects range from seagrass blades and mangrove prop roots to rock and coral reef formations for adults (664; 2410; 2413; 993; 2401).  Jewfish will also associate with manmade structures such as shipwrecks and docks (2403; 2401).  Eggs and larvae are planktonic over the continental shelf dispersing from specific spawning sites (2403; 2401).
Substrate:  Juveniles occur over sand or mud in association with mangroves and seagrass (993; 2401).

nodes.title: Physical/chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: This is a relatively euryhaline/euryoecious species compared to other serranids.  Recorded from salinities of 0.0-39.1 ppt (700; 2405; 789; 2411; Loftus and Kushlan 1987)
Temperatures: temperatures range 18.5-30.0 C (2407).  Sensitive to hypothermal stress with mortality observed at 6.0-13.0 C (2146).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Possibly gonochoristic (at present, no major evidence of protogyny (2401; 2402)), although Smith (1971) considered simultaneous occurrence of oocytes in testicular tissue to be evidence for protogyny (these criteria for protogyny are now suspect (Sadovy and Shapiro 1987)); polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally during simultaneous mating in the water column (2403).
Mating/Spawning Spawning occurs on new and full moons at specific sites associated with reef or wreck formations (2403; 2401; 2402).  Ephemeral color dimorphism and sound production occurs in association with intersexual and social behaviors in spawning aggregations (2403).  Observations of spawning activity and ripe females coincide from June to October in Florida waters (2408; 2403; 2401).
Fecundity: Batch fecundity estimates for two female jewfish (1,322 mm and 1,397 mm TL) were 38,922,168 + 1,518,283 and 56,599,306 + 1,866,130 oocytes, respectively) (2401).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  There are no descriptions of jewfish eggs and larvae (2365), however, epinepheline eggs and larvae are typically planktonic, spherical with a narrow perivitelline space and smooth egg envelope, and range between 0.5 and 1.0 mm in diameter with a single oil globule (2404; 2412).
Larvae:  Epinepheline larvae (4.0-20.0 mm TL) are easily recognized by three very elongate spines, the 2nd dorsal spine, pelvic spine and preopercular spine (at angle), all with serrations (2404; 2412).  It is assumed that jewfish larvae will follow the larval descriptions of Epinephelus species examined to date.  Hatching in Epinephelus spp. usually takes place within 24 hrs with newly hatched larvae ranging from 1.5-1.7 mm in length remaining in the plankton for 30 to 40 days, settling at 20 to 35 mm in benthic continental shelf and estuarine habitats (2412).  It is anticipated that jewfish settlement occurs in seagrass or mangrove forest habitats due to the presence of early juveniles in these habitats (993; 2401).
Juvenile:  Juveniles range from 20 to 1150 mm TL for males, 4-6 yrs of age, whereas females first mature 1200-1350 mm TL at age 6 or 7 (2402).
Adults:  Maturation occurs at 1150-1350 mm TL (2402).  Age is 4-7 yrs at maturation with both the smallest and largest mature individuals being males and latest maturing individuals being females causing some authors to question protogyny in this species (2401; 2402).  Opaque sagittae bands are annuli and demonstrate most rapid growth through age 6 (>100 mm/yr), 30 mm/yr by age 15, 10 mm/yr after age 25 (2402).  Males range 3-26 yrs (795-2057 mm TL), females 0-37 yrs (338-2155 mm TL) and undetermined sex 0-36 yrs (75-2160 mm TL)(2402).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Larvae: larvae are presumed to be planktivorous.
Juvenile: juvenile jewfish prey on penaeid and xanthid crustaceans and fish (2401)
Adult: adults prey on molluscs (octopus, gastropods, and lobsters (Panulirus and Scyllarides), crabs (portunid and xanthids), fishes (Dasyatis, Etrumeus, Chaetodipterus, Diodon, Lactophrys, Chilomycterus; 2401).  Therefore, jewfish are top predators on a variety of reef invertebrates and fishes, though there appears to be some bias toward slow moving or sedentary prey species.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Due to its large size the jewfish has the capacity to influence a variety of prey species within its foraging range.  However, this range appears to be limited as solitary individuals appear to inhabit particular reef locations for prolonged periods (2401).  Limited movement and a varied diet allow jewfish to impact populations of a wide variety of invertebrate and vertebrate species on a particular reef.
Factors Influencing Populations:  As jewfish are slow growing, long lived and sedentary they are particularly vulnerable to overfishing which is believed to be one of the principal causes of adult mortality (2401; 2402).  Therefore, in order to maintain viable reproducing populations of jewfish, fishing mortality must be limited, particularly at spawning sites.

Commercial:  Food fish throughout its range and sold as grouper in limited commercial fishery (2401).  Fishery managers of Florida territorial and U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone waters have recognized the jewfish's susceptibility to overfishing and have recently banned (1990) all harvest of jewfish from waters under their jurisdictions (2402).
Recreational:  Historically easily captured by anglers and SCUBA divers, but now banned (1990) from sport fishery in Florida waters (2401; 2402).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Introduction:  Jewfish are one of the largest teleostean top predators within the Indian River Lagoon and adjacent waters, commonly encountered in ocean inlets, mangrove forests, seagrass meadows and nearshore ocean reefs (848, 993).  Juveniles occur around structures within the lagoon, such as seagrass, mangrove prop roots and rock ledges (2365).  Adults prefer structures associated with deeper water (generally over 3 m depths, but less than 55 m) both within the lagoon and adjacent continental shelf (2401).  Due to its size and broad diet of crustaceans and fishes (2389; 2361; 2401) jewfish may influence mortality rates in certain crustacean and fish populations where it is common as an apical predator.
Indicator:  None known.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Commonly encountered on reef formations from eastern Florida, Gulf of Mexico to southeastern Brazil and in the eastern Pacific from Costa Rica to Peru (2401).  Extralimital occurrence to Virginia (2406).
Within Study Area:  Occurs in Indian River Lagoon seagrass and mangrove estuarine habitats, particularly as a juvenile (848, 993), primarily south of 28 00'N.  Adults are found in deeper basins within the Indian River Lagoon typically near ocean inlets and on nearshore ocean reefs at depths less than 55 m (848; Gilmore, 1972-84 unpubl. field notes Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution).
Life Mode:  A very large solitary residential neritic and estuarine ambush predator (size to 317 kg and over 1.8 m SL: Smith 1971).  Forms predictable aggregations during spawning around reef structure on the continental shelf (2403; 2401).  Highly vulnerable to fishery pressure due to slow growth, longevity, and presumed low natural mortality as populations of cohorts reach maximum biomass at relatively old ages (2402).
Mobility and Migration: Adults make limited migrations to spawning sites and are otherwise relatively sedentary with single individuals having been observed at specific reef formations over multiple annual cycles (2410; 2403; 2401; 2402).  Juveniles move from coastal and estuarine nursery grounds to deeper estuarine or continental shelf reefs upon maturation (2402).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Epinephelus itajara associates with objects rising above the ocean or estuarine bottom as newly settled post larvae or juveniles.  These objects range from seagrass blades and mangrove prop roots to rock and coral reef formations for adults (664; 2410; 2413; 993; 2401).  Jewfish will also associate with manmade structures such as shipwrecks and docks (2403; 2401).  Eggs and larvae are planktonic over the continental shelf dispersing from specific spawning sites (2403; 2401).
Substrate:  Juveniles occur over sand or mud in association with mangroves and seagrass (993; 2401).

sections.heading: Physical/chemical
sections.content:
Salinity: This is a relatively euryhaline/euryoecious species compared to other serranids.  Recorded from salinities of 0.0-39.1 ppt (700; 2405; 789; 2411; Loftus and Kushlan 1987)
Temperatures: temperatures range 18.5-30.0 C (2407).  Sensitive to hypothermal stress with mortality observed at 6.0-13.0 C (2146).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Possibly gonochoristic (at present, no major evidence of protogyny (2401; 2402)), although Smith (1971) considered simultaneous occurrence of oocytes in testicular tissue to be evidence for protogyny (these criteria for protogyny are now suspect (Sadovy and Shapiro 1987)); polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally during simultaneous mating in the water column (2403).
Mating/Spawning Spawning occurs on new and full moons at specific sites associated with reef or wreck formations (2403; 2401; 2402).  Ephemeral color dimorphism and sound production occurs in association with intersexual and social behaviors in spawning aggregations (2403).  Observations of spawning activity and ripe females coincide from June to October in Florida waters (2408; 2403; 2401).
Fecundity: Batch fecundity estimates for two female jewfish (1,322 mm and 1,397 mm TL) were 38,922,168 + 1,518,283 and 56,599,306 + 1,866,130 oocytes, respectively) (2401).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  There are no descriptions of jewfish eggs and larvae (2365), however, epinepheline eggs and larvae are typically planktonic, spherical with a narrow perivitelline space and smooth egg envelope, and range between 0.5 and 1.0 mm in diameter with a single oil globule (2404; 2412).
Larvae:  Epinepheline larvae (4.0-20.0 mm TL) are easily recognized by three very elongate spines, the 2nd dorsal spine, pelvic spine and preopercular spine (at angle), all with serrations (2404; 2412).  It is assumed that jewfish larvae will follow the larval descriptions of Epinephelus species examined to date.  Hatching in Epinephelus spp. usually takes place within 24 hrs with newly hatched larvae ranging from 1.5-1.7 mm in length remaining in the plankton for 30 to 40 days, settling at 20 to 35 mm in benthic continental shelf and estuarine habitats (2412).  It is anticipated that jewfish settlement occurs in seagrass or mangrove forest habitats due to the presence of early juveniles in these habitats (993; 2401).
Juvenile:  Juveniles range from 20 to 1150 mm TL for males, 4-6 yrs of age, whereas females first mature 1200-1350 mm TL at age 6 or 7 (2402).
Adults:  Maturation occurs at 1150-1350 mm TL (2402).  Age is 4-7 yrs at maturation with both the smallest and largest mature individuals being males and latest maturing individuals being females causing some authors to question protogyny in this species (2401; 2402).  Opaque sagittae bands are annuli and demonstrate most rapid growth through age 6 (>100 mm/yr), 30 mm/yr by age 15, 10 mm/yr after age 25 (2402).  Males range 3-26 yrs (795-2057 mm TL), females 0-37 yrs (338-2155 mm TL) and undetermined sex 0-36 yrs (75-2160 mm TL)(2402).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Larvae: larvae are presumed to be planktivorous.
Juvenile: juvenile jewfish prey on penaeid and xanthid crustaceans and fish (2401)
Adult: adults prey on molluscs (octopus, gastropods, and lobsters (Panulirus and Scyllarides), crabs (portunid and xanthids), fishes (Dasyatis, Etrumeus, Chaetodipterus, Diodon, Lactophrys, Chilomycterus; 2401).  Therefore, jewfish are top predators on a variety of reef invertebrates and fishes, though there appears to be some bias toward slow moving or sedentary prey species.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation:  Due to its large size the jewfish has the capacity to influence a variety of prey species within its foraging range.  However, this range appears to be limited as solitary individuals appear to inhabit particular reef locations for prolonged periods (2401).  Limited movement and a varied diet allow jewfish to impact populations of a wide variety of invertebrate and vertebrate species on a particular reef.
Factors Influencing Populations:  As jewfish are slow growing, long lived and sedentary they are particularly vulnerable to overfishing which is believed to be one of the principal causes of adult mortality (2401; 2402).  Therefore, in order to maintain viable reproducing populations of jewfish, fishing mortality must be limited, particularly at spawning sites.
